newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS -- BT may seek MCI price cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -- BT may seek MCI price cut.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc may seek a price cut in its $24 billion merger with MCI Communications Corp after MCI said costs tied to its move into local telephone markets will hurt profits through 1998.

Takeover experts and traders said Friday that BT would be justified in calling MCI back to the bargaining table to reduce the terms, which currently value each MCI share at 0.54 BT American Depositary Receipt, plus a US$6 cash payment.

BT said after MCI issued its profit warning last night that it could not rule out a possible renegotiation, while MCI said it expects the transaction, unvieled last November, to proceed a planned and close by the fall.

The combination of the second-largest U.S. long distance phone company and BT is the biggest transatlantic deal in history, and would create a telecommunications giant named Concert Plc, with annual revenues over $42 billion and 43 million business and residential customers in 70 countries.

It is highly unlikely the combination will unravel altogether, sources agreed, noting the advantage of MCI revealing its local-phone woes prior to the deal's close versus a more devastasting, post-consummation bombshell that could postpone, or nullify, Concert's success.

"This is the time that mergers begin to fall apart because people don't take a second look at the numbers. It is not uncommon for the first pass at the financials to miss these intricate, complicated issues," said John McCreight, president of McCreight & Co, merger strategy implementation consultants.

Renegotiating merger considerations "is relatively simple compared to a (post-close) disaster. It is a simple matter to reconvene the appropriate management and analytical people and redo the business model, get on with a new look at the numbers and learn from it."

"This is definitely a material adverse change, and they (BT) clearly have the leverage to, at the very least, cut the price. So I think the deal gets cut. Though it can be killed, but I don't think that is likely," said an arbitrageur who asked not to be identified.
MCI said 1997 local telephone market losses could reach $800 million, more than twice what was originally planned, with most of the losses coming in the second half of the year.
Losses in the local business in 1998 could exceed the levels incurred in 1997, MCI also said.
As it cast doubt over the BT deal, the news crushed the shares of both companies and triggered MCI earnings estimate reductions by analysts.
In late Nasdaq trade, MCI shares fell 6-3/4 to 35-5/8, a 16 percent loss, with over 30 million shares traded. The retreat put the stock at a three-and-a-half month low.
When the merger was announced early last November, MCI share were trading at around 25.
Meanwhile, BT's NYSE-listed ADRs were off 5-3/16 late Friday, or 6.4 percent, to 76-3/8.
BT ADRs where trading at about 57 when the deal was announced.
Prudential Securities lowered its recommendation on MCI to hold from buy, and Salomon Bros analyst Jack Grubman kept his buy rating but made significant cuts in his earnings outlook.
Grubman lowered the 1997 estimate to $1.15 per share from $1.60 and the 1998 forecast to $1.30 per share from $2.15.
